w: HN treats it as the standard one-hour teaser for the book and recommends it for its deep-modules thinking before buying or reading the book.

t: Defcon 18   Changing threats to privacy   Moxie Marlinspike   Part
q: I would highly encourage anyone who thinks that the solution is as simple as "don't use XYZ" to see what Moxie Marlinspike had to say
w: Cited repeatedly to rebut 'just don't use Facebook' arguments and to explain why tracking becomes hard to escape at critical mass.

t: "Uncle" Bob Martin - "The Future of Programming"
q: It's a fascinating introduction to the evolution of hardware and programming languages.
w: HN recommends it as an engaging overview of programming history and an argument for professional standards, citing the agile manifesto section and the claim that software has advanced little since the 1950s.

t: The Thirty Million Line Problem
q: The video is long, but it's worth watching all of it.
w: HN recommends it, long as it is, as an eye-opening rant on software complexity and why systems became so complicated.

t: CppCon 2017: Matt Kulukundis “Designing a Fast, Efficient, Cache-friendly Hash Table, Step by Step”
q: Excellent talk which explains the concepts really clearly and concisely.
w: HN repeatedly cites it as the definitive explanation of SwissTable, the design behind Abseil, Rust's hash map and Go's maps.

t: The Cardboard Box Reform - Nixon's Ghost Bill & A Crucial Flaw in Democracy
q: It is long, but well-reasoned and supported by a lot of evidence. Definitely worth a watch...
w: HN commenters recommend it as a long, evidence-backed theory for what changed in the 1970s and why Congress is broken, even when they are unsure they agree.

t: Effective Programs - 10 Years of Clojure - Rich Hickey
q: Whole video is gold, is my fav programming talk of all time.
w: HN's go-to link in typing debates and for talk lists, and several call it their favorite programming talk even for non-Clojure users.

t: Brian Goetz - Stewardship: the Sobering Parts
q: Brian Goetz's talk nails it on the head why the languages in my day-to-day are sub-optimal
w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the definitive explanation of why Java evolves cautiously and why compatibility matters in language design.

t: Music and Life - Alan Watts
q: You haven't been failing, you've been dancing.
w: HN commenters post it in threads about purpose, ambition, burnout and career anxiety as a reframing that life is a dance, not a march toward eventual happiness.

t: VCF East: Ken Thompson interviewed by Brian Kernighan
q: Also I found these fascinating
w: HN commenters recommend it for Thompson's funny, first-hand Unix history stories, some of which even Kernighan had not heard.

t: AWS re:Invent 2018: Amazon DynamoDB Deep Dive: Advanced Design Patterns for DynamoDB (DAT401)
q: I highly recommend every engineer to watch it: it's a great overview of SQL vs NoSQL
w: The go-to recommendation for learning DynamoDB data modeling, with many saying it made access-pattern-driven design click.

t: Harder Drive: Hard drives we didn't want or need
q: recommend this video to anyone here.
w: HN treats it as a favorite example of silly but educational computer science, recommended often when threads touch odd storage hacks.

t: Breakthrough in  Nuclear Fusion? - Prof. Dennis Whyte
q: I highly recommend watching Dr. Whyte's talks on YouTube, he discusses the challenges, design, and performance in an approachable way.
w: HN points to it as the grounded, approachable explanation of why REBCO magnets changed the outlook for fusion.

t: The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously.
q: It's got some great graphics and visualisations, and is accessibly narrated.
w: HN strongly recommends it as the clearest, best-illustrated explanation of the solar gravitational lens idea, and links it whenever exoplanet imaging comes up.

t: The Real Story Behind Wayland and X - Daniel Stone (linux.conf.au 2013)
q: incredibly funny and educational talk[1] from 2013
w: HN treats it as the definitive, funny and educational answer to why X could not be fixed, and links it in almost every Wayland vs X argument.

t: Lecture 1 | Machine Learning (Stanford)
q: I'd suggest going back to the original youtube[1] and course materials[2].
w: Recommended as the rigorous, math-heavy original course, deeper than the Coursera version, for learning machine learning.

t: Ruby Midwest 2011 - Keynote: Architecture the Lost Years by Robert Martin
q: The talk that had the most influence on how I write software is Robert 'Uncle Bob' Martin's "Architecture: The Lost Years
w: Frequently recommended as an influential talk on decoupled, testable architecture, though some commenters push back on Martin's TDD advocacy.

t: Confessions of a Converted Lecturer: Eric Mazur
q: Great video on how a pretty good teacher (as conventionally measured) learned how to really teach.
w: Repeatedly recommended in education threads as the definitive talk on why lectures fail and what works better.

t: Hamming, "You and Your Research" (June 6, 1995)
q: So much sage advice as compiled over a very long and fruitful career.
w: HN recommends it as career and research advice on choosing important problems and doing first-class work.

t: RustConf 2018 - Closing Keynote - Using Rust For Game Development by Catherine West
q: is still my favorite ECS explanation, because she builds the concept piece by piece starting from megaclass-hell to full entities-as-IDs with reasons for each step.
w: HN treats it as the go-to explanation of ECS, valuable even for people who don't use Rust.

t: Erlang Factory 2014 - That's 'Billion' with a 'B': Scaling to the Next Level at WhatsApp
q: watch this talk and imagine trying to recreate that system with only a handful of server engineers
w: The go-to talk showing how Erlang let a tiny team run a massive messaging system.

t: Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek - The Original Economics Rap Battle!
q: the Keynes vs. Hayek rap is incredibly well informed about both positions, and it's pretty easy to follow and entertaining
w: HN recommends it as a funny, accurate and easy primer on Keynesian versus Austrian views of the business cycle.

t: A Tour of the Acme Editor
q: Russ Cox has a great video tour of Acme's features here
w: HN points people to it as the best introduction to Acme and its very different take on editors, shells, and GUIs.

t: A Deep Dive into Nanite Virtualized Geometry
q: This siggraph session will expand your mind
w: HN treats it as the definitive deep dive on Nanite, admired for the engineering ambition behind pixel-sized triangles and compute-driven rendering.

t: Hammock Driven Development - Rich Hickey
q: Both of these talks are in my top 5.
w: HN returns to it constantly as permission and method for thinking deeply before coding, and as an antidote to always-working anxiety.

w: HN treats it as the classic demonstration of how analog mechanical computation works, especially the differential gear section.

t: JavaScript: The Good Parts
q: This video changed my mind
w: A classic recommended to people learning JavaScript, even though some find it dogmatic and dated.

t: The Ingenious Design of the Aluminum Beverage Can

w: It is a go-to recommendation whenever cans, good design or mass-produced objects come up, and many also recommend the whole channel.

t: How Crash Bandicoot Hacked The Original Playstation | War Stories | Ars Technica
q: Immensely interesting video!
w: It is one of the most frequently recommended videos on HN for old-school game development hacks under tight hardware constraints.

t: MarI/O - Machine Learning for Video Games
q: his brief videos give a really nice introduction to the topic that should be accessible to most people
w: The go-to accessible introduction to neuroevolution and NEAT, praised for crediting prior research.

t: A Mind Is Born (256 bytes)
q: not only because it is 256 bytes, but because it is a compelling song too.
w: It is HN's favorite example of extreme code compression, a compelling song and visuals from a program smaller than a tweet.

t: Why This Channel Exists (and why I hate Houston)

w: Strongly recommended as the entry point to a channel on urban planning and car dependency in North America.

t: The Loving Trap

t: Tech Talk: Linus Torvalds on git

w: HN repeatedly recommends it as the iconic explanation of why git is designed as it is and why distributed VCS beats centralized ones.

t: Why American Cities Are Broke - The Growth Ponzi Scheme [ST03]

w: HN keeps pointing to it as the clearest explanation of how low-density infrastructure is financed and why it is unsustainable.

t: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

t: Alan Kay's tribute to Ted Nelson at "Intertwingled" Festival

t: The Century of the Self - Part 1: "Happiness Machines"

t: Jonathan Blow - How to program independent games -  CSUA Speech

t: Tim Ewald - Clojure: Programming with Hand Tools
q: I loved this talk on how as your tooling becomes more complex and automated, you start to lose sight of simpler solutions to problems.

t: Brian Beckman: Don't fear the Monad

t: The Coming Collapse of the Middle Class with Elizabeth Warren

t: The Problem With Facebook

t: "How NOT to Measure Latency" by Gil Tene

t: Joe Rogan Experience #1035 - Paul Stamets

w: HN recommends it as the canonical presentation of 'functional core, imperative shell' and a practical answer to unit versus integration testing.

t: USENIX ATC '21/OSDI '21 Joint Keynote Address-It's Time for Operating Systems to Rediscover Hardware

t: Using Python to Code by Voice

t: Clasp: Common Lisp using LLVM and C++ for Molecular Metaprogramming

w: HN repeatedly cites it as a striking example of Common Lisp used to push the frontier of science, and as one of the most inspiring tech talks.

t: Personal Growth Series: Dr. William Dement on Healthy Sleep and Optimal Perfo...

t: Marty Lobdell - Study Less Study Smart

t: Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python
q: the excellent talk "Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python".
w: HN treats it as a must-watch classic for writing Pythonic code, though somewhat dated for modern Python.

t: Shenzhen: The Silicon Valley of Hardware (Full Documentary) | Future Cities | WIRED

t: The essence of calculus

w: A staple recommendation for anyone learning math, praised for visual intuition that makes memorized formulas make sense.

t: How to Do 90% of What Plugins Do (With Just Vim)

t: The Wrong Way to Set Speed Limits [ST06]

w: Recommended again and again in traffic-safety threads as an eye-opener on road design versus posted limits and driver behavior.

t: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever?

w: HN repeatedly calls it a fantastic explanation that made FFT click, with some rewatching it periodically.

t: Dick Proenneke in Alone in the Wilderness
q: I think HN would really appreciate the story of Dick Proenneke
w: HN recommends it often and warmly, as an inspiring and peaceful view of self-reliance and handcraft, in threads on cabins, solitude and woodworking.

t: Mike Monteiro: F*ck You, Pay Me
q: I watched this video from Mike Monteiro and I always refer to it since.
w: HN regulars send freelancers and consultants to it whenever clients don't pay or contracts come up.

t: We the People, and the Republic we must reclaim | Lawrence Lessig

w: HN cites it repeatedly as the root-cause argument that money in politics must be fixed before other issues, and as background for his Mayday PAC.

t: Spec-ulation Keynote - Rich Hickey

t: Modern Dictionaries by Raymond Hettinger

t: Refterm Lecture Part 1 - Philosophies of Optimization

w: HN returns to it constantly in software performance debates as the primer on non-pessimization and why modern software is slow.

t: "Money doesn't interest me" - Ton Roosendaal 2017 Interview

w: Recommended as the best account of Blender's history and its user-focused approach as a free software success story.

t: CppCon 2014: Mike Acton "Data-Oriented Design and C++"

t: Why Your Vote Doesn't Count

t: Siggraph2019 Geometric Algebra

t: The Mother of All Demos, presented by Douglas Engelbart (1968)

w: HN treats it as an essential piece of computing history that shows how many modern interface ideas were already solved in 1968.

t: RSA ANIMATE: Changing Education Paradigms
q: One of my favorite videos on reforming education
w: HN recommends it as an accessible, widely shared critique of schooling, and cites it in threads on ADHD, creativity and education reform.

t: RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning

t: Lecture 6: Version Control (git) (2020)

t: Mindfulness with Jon Kabat-Zinn

t: Is Most Published Research Wrong?

w: HN commenters link it whenever a shaky study or the p<0.05 threshold comes up, as a short primer on false positives in science.

t: How I program C

w: HN recommends it as the one long programming video worth watching, a provocative and influential take on C.

t: The Extreme Engineering of ASML’s EUV Light Source

w: Commenters repeatedly point to it whenever EUV, ASML or chip manufacturing comes up, as a clear and astonishing explanation of one of the hardest engineering problems in chipmaking.

t: 30 Essential Ideas you should know about ADHD, 1A Intro, Chronic Developmental Disability

w: HN commenters repeatedly recommend Barkley's lectures as the best introduction to understanding ADHD.

t: Cities Aren't Loud: Cars Are Loud

t: The Secret War

t: Category Theory 1.1: Motivation and Philosophy

t: "Propositions as Types" by Philip Wadler

w: HN regards it as an entertaining and eye-opening introduction to why logic and functional programming are connected, and it is a frequent pick in favorite-tech-talk threads.

t: Why Some Diseases Only Traveled One Direction

w: HN commenters point to it as a clear, short explanation of one-directional disease spread and the core argument of Guns, Germs, and Steel.

t: This Is What Winning Looks Like (Full Length)

w: Recommended during Afghanistan withdrawal threads as a sobering look at why the transition to local forces was failing.

t: Richard Feynman Fire

t: Jim Keller: Moore's Law, Microprocessors, and First Principles | Lex Fridman Podcast #70

w: HN cites it whenever chip architecture, Moore's Law or CPU design comes up, as an unusually deep and accessible view from a top designer.

t: Object-Oriented Programming is Bad

w: HN returns to it as the go-to critique of OOP, recommended for explaining the costs of abstraction better than most written arguments.

t: The Language of the System - Rich Hickey

t: Why Canadians Can't Bike in the Winter (but Finnish people can)

t: Dr. Robert Zubrin with a brilliant answer to "Why Should We Go To Mars?"
